title: A House for the Visitor
premise: Mirabel Sandoval, an urban explorer obsessed with mapping the unmapped, discovers a tunnel network beneath the drowned town of Harrow's Bend that appears on no survey — and begins documenting it as a ritual of belonging. His sleep recordings reveal a second voice answering his questions in his own cadence, a thing that was invited into his family line generations ago and has been waiting for someone to finally listen. As the harvest moon rises, Mirabel must survive one night inside the house his grandmother sealed shut, holding out until sunrise while learning the truth: the visitor was never haunting the Sandovals — they were keeping it fed so it would never need a body. In the end, Mirabel chooses inheritance over escape, taking his grandmother's place as keeper, and the house lets him go at dawn only because he agrees to come back.
about_author: Lior Kavanagh is the pen name of a former land surveyor who spent a decade mapping decommissioned infrastructure across the American Northeast before turning to fiction. Their work explores what families bury, literally and otherwise, and has appeared in several small-press horror anthologies.

chapters.title: The Survey That Isn't
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. He maps a storm drain outside Harrow's Bend that extends far past its recorded length, documenting every turn with obsessive care. The emotional beat is thrill curdling into unease when his measurements contradict themselves on the way back.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Prayer
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. Flashbacks establish his childhood in his grandmother Odile's sealed house and his compulsion to record everything. He sets up audio equipment to capture ambient sound in the tunnels. The beat is tenderness toward ritual, and loneliness beneath it.

chapters.title: Second Voice
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. Reviewing overnight recordings from the tunnel mouth, he hears himself asking questions he never asked aloud — and something else answering in his own voice. The beat is cold dread arriving quietly, like frost.

chapters.title: What Grandmother Sealed
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. He returns to the boarded-up Sandoval house and finds Odile's journals hidden under floorboards, written in a shorthand mixing survey notation and prayer. The beat is grief mixed with betrayal as he realizes she documented too.

chapters.title: Questions Answered
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. He deliberately asks questions aloud at the tunnel entrance; the recordings return answers about 'the harvest' and 'the keeper.' The beat is the intoxication of contact — he feels seen for the first time.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Remembers
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. Elderly townsperson Ruth Ackley warns him off, revealing that Sandoval men have gone missing near the moon's rise for three generations. The beat is community as warning system, and his stubborn dismissal of it.

chapters.title: Invited In
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. A journal entry reveals Odile's confession: the family invited the visitor in during the flood of 1938 to save the town, and the debt renews each harvest moon. The beat is horror of inheritance — a contract signed before he was born.

chapters.title: Sleepwalking Toward the House
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. He wakes on the porch of the sealed house with mud on his boots and no memory of walking there. The recordings show him speaking all night. The beat is loss of bodily sovereignty, terror turned inward.

chapters.title: Ruth's Bargain
chapters.summary: POV Ruth (one chapter). She recounts her own sister's disappearance decades ago and shows Mirabel the only rule that matters: hold out until sunrise inside the house without answering anything. The beat is reluctant alliance, hope with a price tag.

chapters.title: Preparations
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. He stocks the house, chalks thresholds, sets cameras on every room, and writes instructions to be found if he fails. The beat is grim competence — documentation as armor now, not prayer.

chapters.title: Moonrise
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. The harvest moon rises; the boards breathe; doors he locked stand open onto hallways that shouldn't fit the house. The beat is threshold dread, the ordinary made geometrical wrongness.

chapters.title: The Voice Wears Him Well
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. The visitor speaks through the house in his mother's voice, then Odile's, offering comfort and answers. He nearly responds twice. The beat is aching temptation — grief weaponized.

chapters.title: Rooms That Remember
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. Hallways rearrange to replay family memories: the flood, the first invitation, Odile as a girl feeding something at the cellar door. The beat is vertigo of inherited memory, belonging as a trap.

chapters.title: First Blood Price
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. The house demands a token answer; when he stays silent, it takes his recording equipment instead, erasing hours of footage. The beat is rage and helplessness — his archive devoured.

chapters.title: The Long Middle Hours
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. 2 a.m. to 4 a.m.: silence, then scratching inside the walls spelling his name in survey shorthand. He recites measurements aloud to stay anchored. The beat is endurance, mind fraying but holding.

chapters.title: Odile's Last Entry
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. He finds the journal's final page: Odile didn't die — she went down to renew the lease herself, buying the family twenty more years. Those twenty years end tonight. The beat is devastating clarity about his inheritance.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. Near dawn's edge, the visitor offers him everything: belonging, answers, his grandmother back — if he only says yes. The beat is the story's moral crux, desire dressed as homecoming.

chapters.title: Sunrise Refusal
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. He refuses — but not by silence; he answers with a question of his own, breaking the contract's grammar. Light floods the halls; the house screams in survey notation. The beat is triumphant defiance through wit, not force.

chapters.title: What Walked Out
chapters.summary: POV Ruth. She watches Mirabel emerge changed — calmer, older-eyed — carrying Odile's journal and a new page written in his hand. The beat is wary relief; survivors are never quite the same shape.

chapters.title: Terms of Keeping
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. He deciphers the renegotiated terms: the visitor will wait, fed by documentation instead of bodies, as long as a Sandoval keeps the records. The beat is sober acceptance — he has traded escape for stewardship.

chapters.title: A House for the Visitor
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. He repairs the house, installs new recording equipment, and writes the first entry of the next twenty years. The beat is quiet devotion transformed — the prayer continues, but now he knows to whom.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon, Next Year
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel, final pages. One year later, he walks the tunnels openly, mapping them at last, and leaves the cellar door unlocked on purpose. The last line of his log: 'Expecting company.' The beat is peace laced with dread — belonging fully chosen.
